items.title: 3.2 Electronegativity and the type of bond

source_refs.note: Topic 3.2, printed page 50 (Figure 3.4), with Quick Check 3.3 as the self-check.

blocks.text: Electronegativity was discussed in chapter 1; here its effect on the type of bonding is considered. The difference in electronegativity of two bonded atoms gives an approximate measure of the bond polarity and an indication of the type of bond. When the difference is very small or zero the bond is covalent and non-polar; when it is large the bond is polar covalent or ionic. Two atoms with an electronegativity difference below 0.4 make a pure covalent bond; a difference between 0.4 and 1.8 corresponds to a polar covalent bond; above this the bond is ionic in nature. The differences for H-H, H-Cl and NaCl are 0 (non-polar), 0.9 (polar covalent) and 2.1 (ionic), which is why H-H is purely non-polar, H-Cl is a polar covalent bond and NaCl is an ionic compound.

blocks.caption: Bond type from the electronegativity difference (Figure 3.4)

blocks.alt: A horizontal scale from 0 to above 1.8 shaded blue to red and marked pure covalent, polar covalent and ionic with H-H, H-Cl and NaCl placed on it. Below: an HF molecule with its electron cloud shifted to fluorine and an arrow from H to F, bent H2O and SO2 molecules with net arrows, and linear BeCl2 and trigonal BF3 with opposing arrows that cancel.
blocks.caption: Electronegativity difference, bond type and dipole moments (original diagram after Figures 3.4 to 3.7).
blocks.long_description: A difference under 0.4 gives a pure covalent bond, 0.4 to 1.8 a polar covalent bond and above 1.8 an ionic bond. In HF the shared electrons lie nearer fluorine, so hydrogen is delta+ and fluorine delta-, and the dipole moment points from H to F. In angular molecules such as H2O (1.85 D) and SO2 (1.61 D) the bond moments add to a net moment; in symmetrical BeCl2, BF3, CH4 and CCl4 equal bond moments in a regular geometry cancel to zero.

blocks.prompt: Using electronegativity differences, predict whether the bonds in HF, KI, CaF2, ICl and Br2 are non-polar covalent, polar covalent or ionic.
blocks.explanation: Br2 has a zero difference, so non-polar covalent. ICl has a small difference, under 0.4 to about 0.5 depending on the values used, so pure to slightly polar covalent. HF has a difference of about 1.9 and is strongly polar covalent (close to the ionic border). KI (about 1.7) is on the border and is counted as ionic in practice; CaF2 (about 3.0) is clearly ionic.

items: Electronegativity difference measures bond polarity: below 0.4 pure covalent (H-H, 0), 0.4 to 1.8 polar covalent (H-Cl, 0.9), above 1.8 ionic (NaCl, 2.1).
